item.title: China Open Source Daily — 2026-11-12
item.description: On 2026-11-12 two things happened to China's open-source carve-out at once. The public consultation on Announcement No. 48 closes on 15 November, and MOFCOM's own answers to reporters have already conceded more than the draft text did: open-sourcing AI technology, building your own compute centre abroad, tape-out overseas, joint R&D using foreign resources and international standard-setting all qualify for automatic licensing, described in the ministry's words as 'basically report-and-go'. Meanwhile the registration queue has begun producing results: on 22-23 October CCTV's Yuyuantan and then MiniMax itself disclosed that DeepSeek and MiniMax had completed registration and walked models through open-source release and overseas authorisation. Read together, the carve-out has stopped being a clause and become an administered process with named participants and a published first case. The same fortnight produced the opposite kind of transaction in embodied AI: AgiBot donated its Lingqu OS project to the OpenAtom Foundation as a platinum donor and committed to open-sourcing 200 million lines of production-validated code and 5,000+ packages by year-end, while OpenLET -- the foundation's embodied-intelligence community, seven months old -- reported 70+ co-builders, over 10,000 developers, 100,000+ minutes of real-robot data, and folded an industrial in-the-loop dataset donated by a partner into the shared pool. One is a commons contribution with a unit of account that did not exist before; the other is a licence to publish that now has a queue. Both are the same institutional machine, and the difference between them is the thing worth measuring.
